 This episode places a gigantic bet on Michael and Olivia’s clashing styles amounting to something greater than the sum of their parts.
 Photo: Elizabeth Fisher/CBS 
 There’s one particular shot I love in this week’s Cupertino . The camera is fixed at a corner that connects two hallways in the labyrinthine San Mateo Hall of Justice. Michael and Olivia have been defending two tech bros, A.J. (Ben Cook) and Buddy (Taip Oskar Ćeman), who run a prediction-market website, WagerMode, that the state of California is trying to shut down. But because Michael has been talking to A.J. while Olivia handles Buddy — and because District Attorney Sally Clawson (Amanda Warren) has decided to offer a deal to whichever partner acts first — we get an amusing cut to Michael and Olivia flying down separate hallways, racing away from each other and off into the distance. It’s the whole theme of the episode in one snappy second: Partners zooming off in different directions.
 “A.J. and Buddy” maintains that kind of energy — and visual flair — throughout most of its running time. It’s the closest Cupertino has come yet to doing a true stand-alone episode, with a story that pops up seemingly out of nowhere and then builds and builds for nearly a full 45 minutes. It’s a fantastic episode overall, harmed only by a few momentum-stalling digressions and an ending that feels a little abrupt. Not for the first time (and I’m sure not for the last), I found myself wondering how much better this show could be with another 10 to 15 minutes of running time.
 The case-of-the-week begins with Christy (always a good starting point for any Cupertino ). While clubbing, Christy fixates on a handsome, melancholy lad named A.J. and takes him back to her apartment without learning anything about him, which is understandable, given how many cocky Valley guys she probably encounters on a typical night out. So she’s mildly shocked the next morning when A.J. asks her to give him a ride to the airport, where a private jet is waiting. She’s even more surprised when she’s in the middle of touring the jet and it suddenly takes off for Saint Kitts.
 From there, the story moves very quickly. A.J. explains that he needs Christy’s bosses to race to his house before the cops arrive to retrieve Buddy’s laptop. (They also find their retainer there, in wads of cash stashed among shelves full of shoe boxes and baking-powder cans.) When the police do arrive, what follows is a whirlwind of court appearances and client conferences, all while the DA and her officers try to move as quickly as possible to get what they need from the WagerMode boys — even if it risks violating due process.
 All of this culminates in the kind of twist common to Michelle and Robert King’s legal dramas, where we often eventually discover that there are secret motivations behind what seem like simple cases. When it comes to WagerMode, Michael wants to prove that his client is a victim of selective prosecution, given that another site called PolyBetting runs an almost identical business and has a California gaming license. (It’s implied that PolyBetting does a lot of donating to politicians, including to the Trump family.) As much as DA Clawson tries to claim the moral high ground, noting that WagerMode takes bets on possible political assassinations, she eventually admits this case is really about election interference — and about the million-dollar bets from an anonymous customer: Go4Broke.
 Similarly, this episode is, somewhat slyly, more about partnerships than prediction markets. It’s quite obviously about the title characters, A.J. and Buddy, who met in college and formed a symbiotic business relationship, with A.J. making bold plays while Buddy backs him up with programming genius. Yet A.J. is still a lonely little rich kid. At times he treats Christy like a playdate, offering her Pop-Tarts on a silver platter and asking her to “aisle surf” down his jet during takeoffs. And given the opportunity to betray his only real friend, the aptly named Buddy — who is actually Go4Broke — A.J. hesitates.
 The other partnership examined in this episode is, of course, Michael and Olivia’s. When circumstances divide them, Olivia seizes the opportunity to show Michael that she can be more than just the sneakily sweet half of their dynamic. She defends Buddy fiercely , even getting a cut on her cheek while trying to physically prevent the police from unlocking Buddy’s computer. She also calls out Michael in front of the judge, accusing him of lying when he says he didn’t know A.J. was trying to flee the country. Michael rolls with his partner’s punches, seeing it as ordinary courtroom tussling. Olivia seems more uncertain about the parts they have to play in this case — although she’s quite good at being ruthless.
 As I mentioned, this episode feels somewhat curtailed, with A.J. and Buddy’s case(s) stalling out after WagerMode starts posting odds on Clawson’s reelection. I feel like the issues this story raises — about partnerships and prediction markets — don’t get addressed as fully as they could have been. But hey, this is only episode 4 of a 20-episode season. Perhaps WagerMode will return to extract some more value from the million-dollar gold bar A.J. gave Christy as a retainer.
 Part of me also wishes this episode had stuck with the WagerMode plot exclusively —  although this is no knock against the scenes that keep interrupting the main story, which involve Natalia hanging around the empty PSA offices with a visiting Nichole. (A treat for Girls5Eva fans!) Some important news gets dropped during these interludes, namely that Nichole now represents Colt AI, which is suing PSA for “illegally accessing” Bo.
 It’s also worth noting that as soon as Natalia wanders into the PSA backrooms, she sees the pillar where Michael and Olivia signed their partnership “contract” and adds her own name, with a new 33/33/33 split. Maybe that’s what it will take to keep Price and Siffre united: a third partner they can team up against.
 Would Natalia’s power move hold up in court? Probably not. But as she herself points out, “Lawsuits are just the language of business.” In Silicon Valley, you don’t always go to court for justice. Sometimes you just want the people in your life to listen — really listen — to your complaints.
 Spam Folder 
 • It takes 15 minutes before the opening credits kick in this week. Good to see the Kings up to their old tricks.
 • A big part of what makes this episode so fun is that for the first five minutes or so we’re just hanging out with Christy, who knows how to have a good time. We get to see the half-assed way she handles her wardrobe. (Sometimes she puts her dresses on hangers, but “then I get bored.”) And we get to see her fill her purse with all of the fancy soaps and lotions on A.J.’s PJ. (“I’m more of a Spirit Air kind of girl,” she tells him.)
 • File this away for later: Olivia’s terrible sub-freeway apartment is also right above some guy running video-game servers, which make Olivia’s floor buzz all day.
 • Robert King directed this episode, and one of the hallmarks of his directing style dating back to The Good Wife is his use of off-screen space and implied action, especially when it comes to the kind of technology we all use every day. Case in point: Olivia fights hard to keep the police from using Buddy’s finger to unlock his laptop, and right before the commercial break, as she falls to the floor, we hear the telltale chime of a Mac starting up.
 • Another nice touch from King: the extreme close-ups on A.J. and Christy’s faces while they’re bantering and snacking on his jet. It’s unusually intimate and emphasizes how much A.J. needs close human contact.
 • Another nice touch from the writers (including credited screenwriter Joey Hartstone): When the teetotaling Olivia joins her colleagues in drinking fancy Champagne to celebrate their sort-of win, her reaction to both the alcohol and the success is the same: “Bitter.”
